2609.28049.title: Prompt, Probe, Train, or Annotate? Single-camera sports video understanding in amateur settings
2609.28049.paper_summary: Video understanding is usually benchmarked on curated, single-actor, or professionally filmed clips, and a strong score there is routinely read as evidence a model is robust enough for deployment. Amateur team sport is a useful, largely untested place to check that assumption: over eight million students played a school sport in the United States in 2024-25 alone, almost none of it filmed by more than a single fixed camera, with several candidate actors crowded into frame and no operator or second angle to fall back on. Using volleyball as a test case, we ask whether strong performance on general video and world-model benchmarks translates into reliable, per-player attribution once footage is this chaotic, turning footage into statistics through a chain of tasks from finding play boundaries to naming who did what. We evaluate four approaches (prompting and agentic reasoning over frontier vision-language models, classical computer vision with small trained specialists, self-supervised video world models, and manual annotation) at every stage, on 66 amateur matches with 46,648 human-labelled contacts, filmed under conditions no published benchmark uses. No single paradigm wins every stage, and static, single-frame computer vision is not competitive at any stage involving motion or identity. A prompted model segments matches well, yet a far smaller trained model beats it at spotting contacts for a fraction of the cost, and the sport's own rules recover rally outcomes the pixels cannot. Identity is where every automated approach struggles: a jersey number is a static fact temporal reasoning cannot recover if never visible, unlike sporting action, a repeated motor pattern a temporal model can exploit, which is why holistic reasoning improves event detection while identity stays unchanged. We close with where each approach earns its cost, and what transfers beyond volleyball to amateur sport.
2609.28049.paper_summary_zh: 視頻理解通常是在策劃過的、單一演員或專業拍攝的片段上進行基準測試，並且在這裡取得強勁的分數常常被解讀為模型足夠穩健以便部署。業餘團隊運動是一個有用的、基本上未經測試的地方來檢查這一假設：僅在2024-25年，美國就有超過八百萬名學生參加了校內運動，幾乎沒有超過一個固定攝影機拍攝，幾位候選演員擠在畫面中，沒有操作員或第二個角度可供依賴。我們以排球作為測試案例，詢問在這樣混亂的影片中，對一般視頻和世界模型基準的強勁表現是否能轉化為可靠的每位選手歸因，通過從找到比賽邊界到命名誰做了什麼的一系列任務將影片轉化為統計數據。我們在每個階段評估四種方法（在前沿視覺-語言模型上進行提示和自主推理、使用小型訓練專家進行經典計算機視覺、自我監督視頻世界模型和手動標註），在66場業餘比賽中進行，這些比賽有46,648個人類標註的接觸，拍攝條件與任何已發表的基準都不相同。沒有單一的範式在每個階段都獲勝，靜態的單幀計算機視覺在任何涉及運動或身份的階段都不具競爭力。一個提示模型能很好地分割比賽，然而一個規模小得多的訓練模型在識別接觸方面以更低的成本擊敗了它，而這項運動的規則則恢復了像素無法提供的回合結果。身份是每種自動化方法都掙扎的地方：球衣號碼是一個靜態事實，時間推理無法恢復如果從未可見，這與運動行為不同，後者是一種時間模型可以利用的重複運動模式，這就是為什麼整體推理改善事件檢測而身份保持不變的原因。我們最後總結每種方法的成本收益，以及哪些知識可以轉移到業餘運動之外。
